dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, human-led deployment and materially extends it with workplace evidence that GenAI redistributes cognitive effort toward verification, response integration and stewardship. It also identifies confidence, domain expertise and interaction design as factors shaping whether oversight is meaningful, while appropriately limiting its findings to self-reported associations rather than demonstrated skill loss or causal effects.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s competence-risk proposition by linking GenAI reliance to reduced critical-thinking effort, warning against reserving scrutiny for high-stakes work, and advocating regular practice and system design that sustains users’ awareness, motivation and ability. Its evidence is self-reported and cross-sector rather than legal-workflow-specific, so it reinforces rather than materially extends the cluster.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between perceived usefulness or reduced cognitive effort and objectively measured productivity, learning, or ability. It finds that knowledge workers generally reported lower critical-thinking effort with GenAI, but its self-reported measures do not establish an actual loss of critical-thinking capacity or a causal productivity effect.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s conditional account by associating outcomes during GenAI use with user-specific confidence and by showing that critical thinking shifts toward verification, integration and task stewardship. kp.k: Survey measures perceived thinking, not objectively demonstrated skill loss
kp.d: The 2025 CHI study surveyed 319 knowledge workers recruited through Prolific who used GenAI at work at least weekly, analysing 936 retained examples: 374 Creation, 303 Information and 259 Advice. Participants reported critical thinking in 555 examples (59.29%). The study combined mixed-effects regressions with qualitative coding, measuring perceived manifestations of critical thinking and perceived effort across six Bloom’s taxonomy activities rather than objectively testing cognitive deterioration. These are cross-domain findings, not a representative study of lawyers.

kp.k: Task-specific AI confidence correlates with less critical thinking
kp.d: The authors report a negative association between confidence in AI performing a task and perceived critical-thinking enactment (β=-0.69, p<0.001). Confidence in performing the task independently (β=0.26, p=0.026), confidence in evaluating AI responses (β=0.31, p=0.046), and general reflective tendency (β=0.52, p<0.001) were positively associated with enactment. They found no significant association with overall trust in GenAI and no main effect for the three task categories. Subjective confidence should not be equated with objectively measured expertise.

kp.k: Most examples involve perceived reductions in cognitive effort
kp.d: Reported reductions in effort comprised 72% of Knowledge examples, 79% of Comprehension, 69% of Application, 72% of Analysis, 76% of Synthesis and 55% of Evaluation. Task-specific AI confidence was negatively associated with effort for every activity except Application; self-confidence was positively associated with Application and Evaluation effort. General trust in GenAI was negatively associated with Knowledge, Application, Analysis and Evaluation effort. Reduced effort is not necessarily reduced thinking: the authors identify assistance, cognitive offloading, reduced engagement and confusion between general effort and critical-thinking effort as alternative interpretations.

kp.k: Information gathering shifts toward verification, including in legal research
kp.d: Participants described reduced effort retrieving information at scale (111/319) and obtaining readable organisation (87/319), but increased effort because AI responses can be wrong and require verification (56/319). A lawyer, P147, described using ChatGPT to locate laws and spending valuable time manually checking information it fabricated to support the requested argument. This is a participant’s reported experience, not a measured legal-research error rate. Verification practices included checking referenced sources (23/319) and cross-referencing external sources (114/319).

kp.k: Problem-solving shifts toward integrating AI responses
kp.d: Participants reported that personalised solutions reduced problem-solving effort (77/319), while applying supplied examples to new contexts also helped (9/319). However, applying AI responses to their actual tasks could increase effort (19/319), including adapting marketing tone, checking technical details and fitting generated code into existing systems. One participant reported that adapting generated code ultimately required more effort than doing the work independently; this was an individual experience rather than an average productivity estimate.

kp.k: Task stewardship retains human responsibility despite delegated production
kp.d: The authors describe a shift from execution to oversight: defining intentions, translating them into prompts, steering outputs and assessing quality. Participants reported reduced effort from task scaffolding (48/319), automated creation (129/319) and personalised feedback (40/319), alongside increased effort articulating queries (45/319), steering responses (48/319) and evaluating generated content (42/319). The authors prefer the stewardship metaphor because human users retain responsibility and accountability even when AI produces the material; they do not claim execution disappears entirely.

kp.k: Quality, harm avoidance and learning motivate critical engagement
kp.d: Qualitative themes identify work quality (74/319), potential negative outcomes (116/319) and skill development (13/319) as motivators. Participants checked generic or unsuitable outputs, sought to prevent errors and professional consequences, and sometimes deliberately studied AI corrections to improve their independent performance. Critical-thinking practices extended across goal formation, prompt revision, inspection against objective and subjective criteria, verification, selective incorporation and stylistic adaptation. These counts describe coded participant reports rather than prevalence across the workforce.

kp.k: Trust, workplace incentives and knowledge gaps inhibit scrutiny
kp.d: Reported inhibitors included treating tasks as trivial (55/319), trust and reliance on GenAI (83/319), insufficient time (44/319), and treating scrutiny as outside one’s responsibilities (11/319). Participants also reported difficulty inspecting responses (58/319) and improving them through revised queries (72/319). A sales worker linked limited scrutiny to daily quotas and job security. Some participants doubted their own competence, including in composing legal letters, and accepted AI outputs by default. The authors distinguish awareness, motivation and ability barriers rather than attributing all failures to model reliability.

kp.k: Long-term deskilling is a risk, not a demonstrated outcome
kp.d: Drawing on prior work on skill decay and automation, the authors argue that dispensing with routine critical-thinking practice may leave workers less prepared for exceptional or high-stakes tasks. They warn that restricting scrutiny to high-stakes situations can undermine the practice needed to handle those situations well. Their survey does not demonstrate longitudinal cognitive deterioration or causally establish that GenAI diminishes independent problem-solving; they recommend longitudinal research to investigate changing usage and thinking practices.

kp.k: Training should strengthen oversight while preserving foundational skills
kp.d: The authors recommend training in information verification, response integration and task stewardship, alongside retaining information-gathering and problem-solving skills. Proposed tool designs include proactive prompts when reflection may be overlooked, user-requested critical-thinking assistance, feedback to calibrate confidence, adjustable assistance, guided critiques and support for checking authoritative sources. They suggest presenting critical reflection as professional development rather than merely an additional auditing burden. These are recommendations derived from survey findings, not interventions tested by this study.

kp.k: Self-report and sampling limitations constrain interpretation
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that participants sometimes conflated easier GenAI use with reduced critical-thinking effort, and that subjective task confidence may be poorly calibrated to actual expertise. The survey was exclusively in English and skewed toward younger, technologically skilled regular GenAI users, limiting generalisation to other workers and linguistic contexts. Evolving tools and the broad task taxonomy further limit interpretation. Suggested follow-up methods include think-aloud protocols, task-based assessments, more detailed task measures, longitudinal studies and tool-based experience sampling.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lee et al. report that GenAI generally reduces knowledge workers’ perceived cognitive effort, while task-specific confidence in AI is associated with less reported critical thinking.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain study of knowledge work, not a legal-market study. Participants reported less or much less effort in 72% of applicable examples for Knowledge, 79% for Comprehension, 69% for Application, 72% for Analysis, 76% for Synthesis, and 55% for Evaluation. The authors report a negative association between task-specific confidence in AI and perceived enaction of critical thinking, and positive associations with confidence in performing the task independently and evaluating AI responses. General trust in GenAI is distinct: it was associated with lower perceived effort in four cognitive activities, but not significantly associated with whether critical thinking was reported. These are associations involving self-reports, not measured causal changes in thinking ability.

pts.k: The authors identify a shift from producing work toward verifying, integrating, and overseeing AI output.
pts.d: Their qualitative analysis describes three shifts: information gathering toward information verification; problem-solving toward response integration; and task execution toward task stewardship. GenAI can retrieve and organise information, generate artefacts, scaffold problems, and provide feedback, but workers must check accuracy, adapt output to context, articulate requirements, and steer responses. The authors do not claim that execution disappears or that oversight is wholly new. Their stewardship framing retains human responsibility and accountability despite delegation of production.

pts.k: A lawyer’s account illustrates how fabricated information can add verification work to AI-assisted legal research.
pts.d: Participant P147, identified as a lawyer, described using ChatGPT to find relevant laws for a case and having to spend time manually checking information that the system invented to support the requested argument. Separately, the authors include composing legal letters among tasks where participants’ self-doubt encouraged default acceptance of AI output, citing P204. They warn that reliance can have serious consequences in high-stakes settings such as legal drafting. These are participant experiences and the authors’ risk interpretation, not legal-tool benchmarks, measured hallucination rates, or findings about law-firm staffing and economics.

pts.k: The authors warn of possible long-term overreliance and weakened independent problem-solving, and propose training and design responses.
pts.d: They argue that bypassing routine opportunities to exercise judgement may leave workers less prepared for exceptional, high-stakes tasks. Long-term deterioration is a potential consequence, not an outcome measured by this survey. Conversely, they suggest that developing domain expertise and associated confidence could improve critical engagement with GenAI. Their recommendations include training in verification, response integration, and stewardship; retaining foundational information-gathering and problem-solving skills; and designing tools to address awareness, motivation, and ability barriers. These interventions were proposed rather than tested in this study.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The empirical basis is an online survey of 319 knowledge workers and qualitative and regression analyses of 936 retained examples.
pts.d: Participants were recruited through Prolific and used GenAI at work at least weekly. They described real work tasks and reported critical-thinking practices, perceived effort relative to working without AI, and confidence. The authors report critical thinking in 555 of 936 examples (59.29%). They used a random-intercepts logistic regression for reported enaction and six random-intercepts linear regressions for perceived effort across Bloom’s cognitive activities, accounting for repeated observations by participant and applying a multiple-comparison correction. Qualitative coding supplied accounts of verification, integration, stewardship, and barriers. The claims about future skill decay additionally draw on earlier skill-retention and automation literature. The study did not objectively measure output quality, time savings, legal research accuracy, or longitudinal skill changes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe contemporary, regular workplace GenAI use; the longer-term consequences remain conditional and undated.
pts.d: Published at CHI 2025, the paper presents a baseline for the tools and usage patterns studied rather than a forecast with a specified horizon. Critical engagement varies with task-specific confidence, perceived stakes, time pressure, job responsibilities, and ability to inspect and improve output. The authors acknowledge possible conflation of general effort savings with reduced critical-thinking effort, and that subjective confidence is not necessarily objective expertise. The English-only sample skews toward younger, technologically skilled regular users, limiting generalisation. Lower perceived effort could reflect successful support, offloading, less critical thinking, or confusion between different kinds of effort; it cannot simply be equated with diminished ability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected population is knowledge workers across professions, including lawyers, with implications for users’ organisations and GenAI tool designers.
pts.d: Participants included workers in computing, creative fields, administration, business and finance, education, healthcare, and legal work. Users gain assistance with gathering information and generating content but face checking, contextual adaptation, and oversight demands. Workers with low confidence or insufficient domain knowledge may struggle to challenge output; time-constrained workers and those who regard checking as someone else’s responsibility may not prioritise it. High-stakes professional uses make errors more consequential. The paper recommends training and tool support but does not establish different effects for law-firm partners, associates, in-house counsel, ALSPs, or particular legal-market segments, nor does it predict legal employment or pricing changes.
